title: ECB Economic Bulletin 7/2026 weighs an intensifying energy shock against weaker demand and stable wage growth
summary: The November issue explains the Governing Council's 29 October decision to keep the deposit facility rate at 2.50%, the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. Principal repayments from the two asset purchase portfolios continued to run off. The bulletin records an October assessment, not a new November rate decision. More expensive energy threatened to raise near-term inflation while reducing real household income, spending and investment. Higher market interest rates would restrain demand further. Whether these forces required a change in policy depended partly on how much the energy shock fed into other prices, wages and longer-term expectations.

The jump in headline inflation was larger than the shift in underlying domestic costs. Annual HICP inflation rose from 3.2% in August to 3.8% in September, with energy accelerating from 14.3% to 18.9%. Excluding energy, inflation rose from 2.1% to 2.3%. Services increased from 3.0% to 3.2%, while goods slowed from 1.2% to 1.1%. Compensation per employee grew by 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% in the first. The ECB wage tracker pointed to negotiated growth of 2.5–2.8% in the remaining months of 2026 and an average 2.6% in the first three quarters of 2027. This forward indicator concerns agreements already in the tracker. A sustained increase in later settlements would change the interpretation. Most longer-term inflation expectations remained around 2%.

Activity had expanded unevenly. Statistics Table 2.1 records quarterly real GDP growth of 0.6% in the second quarter, with net trade contributing 0.9 percentage points and domestic demand subtracting 0.3 points. At the assessment date, third-quarter indicators suggested continued expansion. Digital services, manufacturing and exports benefited from AI investment, and public infrastructure and defence spending supported demand. Corporate contacts described cautious consumers trading down, weak demand for some durable goods and higher cost pressure. Unemployment stood at 6.4% in August. Employment and labour-force growth were subdued, while productivity had gradually improved. The expectation of continued expansion was an interpretation of incoming evidence, distinct from the preceding quarter's national accounts.

The credit data showed both tighter supply and weaker demand. In August, firms' market debt cost 4.1% against 4.0% in July, and the composite bank lending rate was 3.8%. Annual corporate loan growth slowed to 4.2% in August and September from 4.4% in July. Corporate debt securities issuance grew 4.2% year on year in September. The October lending survey found that banks tightened business standards in the third quarter because of borrowers' economic risks. Demand for business loans fell despite greater inventory and working-capital needs. Mortgage rates rose to 3.6% in August. Mortgage standards were unchanged, but demand declined substantially. A reduction in loan growth therefore has different explanations across the business and household books.

The eight boxes isolate mechanisms that the aggregates combine. Refined diesel shortages help explain why fuel inflation can rise despite a lower crude assumption. The scenario box finds that a path with GDP growth and inflation held flat can have very little historical precedent even when its cumulative distance from baseline resembles a more plausible adverse scenario. Other boxes distinguish weather interruptions from persistent construction weakness, private care provision from government employment, and corporate contacts from measured activity. The financial boxes examine AI disclosures and corporate financing, how competitive banks transmit policy, and household stablecoins held largely alongside other crypto-assets. Each addresses a different sample and transmission channel.

The two longer articles concern productive capacity and risk over horizons beyond the October meeting. The industrial-policy article explains how targeted intervention can serve public goals while creating fiscal costs or protecting unproductive firms. A subsidy can be ineffective when fragmentation prevents businesses from reaching efficient scale. The climate and nature article describes how physical hazards, the energy transition and nature degradation enter the Eurosystem's economic analysis and risk management. Neither supplies a quantified offset to the current energy shock. The policy reading remains conditional on its duration, wage transmission and the extent to which higher funding costs curb demand.

questions.question: What would distinguish a temporary fuel shock from a persistent increase in underlying inflation?
questions.detail: Track diesel and petrol spreads, negotiated settlements entering the wage tracker, unit labour costs and services prices in successive releases. Compare the sequence with what firms reported about costs and selling prices. This would show whether the market's expected path for short rates is exposed mainly to volatile fuel assumptions or to a more durable shift in domestic inflation.

questions.question: Is weaker business borrowing a funding constraint for otherwise viable firms?
questions.detail: Separate tighter bank standards from customers' response to higher interest costs, and distinguish inventory finance from investment loans. Compare survey responses with bank lending flows, corporate bond issuance and access by firm size. Large companies that can issue securities and smaller bank-dependent borrowers could face quite different refinancing risks despite similar growth rates in aggregate loans and bonds.

questions.question: How much of the apparent resilience in output is likely to support recurring domestic demand?
questions.detail: Reconcile the strong second-quarter trade contribution with later exports, domestic investment, consumer spending and the next national accounts vintage. Compare the firm's exposure to AI-related external demand or public procurement with evidence from companies selling to households. For equity and credit portfolios, this would help distinguish improving underlying customer demand from a temporary favourable contribution to GDP.
